result: PTEN-deficient prostate cancer cells display hyperactivated Akt, elevated oxygen consumption, increased oxidative phosphorylation, and high intracellular ROS levels in an Akt-dependent manner. The study demonstrates that DU145 cells (PTEN-proficient) have low Akt activity and low ROS, while PC3 and LNCaP cells (PTEN-deficient) show hyperactivated Akt with correspondingly higher oxygen consumption and ROS levels. Knockdown of Akt1/Akt2 in PC3 cells decreased both oxygen consumption and ROS levels.
evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C36, C46-C62, C73, and C169 are well-supported by experimental data in Figure 1A-F showing the correlation between PTEN status, Akt activity, oxygen consumption, and ROS levels across three cell lines. The Akt-dependence is demonstrated by knockdown experiments (C52, C53, C59, C60). The data consistently show that PTEN-deficient cells with hyperactive Akt have elevated OXPHO and ROS.

result: High intracellular ROS levels selectively sensitize PTEN-deficient prostate cancer cells displaying hyperactive Akt to ROS-induced cell death. PTEN-deficient PC3 and LNCaP cells were more vulnerable to 2-ME and PEITC-induced cell death than PTEN-proficient DU145 cells. This selectivity results from high ROS levels induced by Akt activation combined with Akt's inability to protect against ROS-induced cell death.
evaluation: Claims C5, C35, C74-C75, C79, C85-C87, C90-C95, C170-C171 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2A-B and supplementary figures showing differential sensitivity to ROS inducers. The mechanistic basis is demonstrated through PTEN manipulation (C90-C91), mAkt expression (C92-C93), and Akt knockdown (C94) experiments. NAC rescue experiments (C87) confirm ROS-dependence.

result: A therapeutic strategy combining the ROS inducer PEITC with rapamycin elicited tumor regression and eradication in PTEN-deficient PC3 xenografts. Rapamycin alone or PEITC alone attenuated tumor growth but tumors remained palpable, while the combination regressed and eradicated tumors. Rapamycin further sensitized cells to ROS-induced death by activating Akt through relief of mTORC1 feedback inhibition, converting rapamycin's cytostatic effect to cytotoxic.
evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C96-C100, C105-C110, C113, C172-C175 are supported by in vitro data (Figure 2D) and xenograft experiments (Figure 2E-H). The combination showed synergistic effects with tumor eradication in PC3 xenografts but not in PTEN-proficient DU145 xenografts (C111-C112), demonstrating selectivity. The mechanism involving rapamycin-induced Akt activation is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 12.

result: Treatment with rapamycin and PEITC in Pbsn-Cre4;Ptenf/f mice (starting at 4 months) significantly decreased prostate weights, markedly inhibited proliferation, induced cell death, and increased survival. The combination was most effective when both drugs were used together. Histopathological analysis showed reduced tumor grade compared to untreated mice.
evaluation: Claims C114-C123 and C134 are supported by experimental data from the Pbsn-Cre4;Ptenf/f mouse model shown in Figure 3. The treatment protocol, prostate weights (Figure 3C), proliferation/death markers (Figure 3D-F), survival data (Figure 3G), and histopathology (Table 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 3) all support the efficacy of the combination therapy. Body weight data (C117-C118) confirm lack of systemic toxicity.

result: Treatment with rapamycin and PEITC in Pbsn-Cre4;Ptenf/f mice starting at 2 months significantly reduced prostate weights and increased survival, with effects sustained even 6 months after treatment cessation. Remarkably, both decreased proliferation and increased cell death persisted 6 months post-treatment, suggesting tumor regression rather than just growth inhibition.
evaluation: Claims C127-C133, C176-C177 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4. The sustained effects after treatment cessation (Figure 4F-I) are particularly striking, with continued decreased BrdU incorporation (C131) and increased cell death (C132) at 12 months. Survival data (Figure 4J) confirms long-term benefit. This suggests the treatment induces durable anti-tumor effects.

result: Exposure to the antioxidant N-acetyl cysteine (NAC) increased prostate tumor progression in Pbsn-Cre4;Ptenf/f mice. NAC treatment markedly increased prostate weights and tumor grade, with all NAC-treated mice developing carcinoma (75% invasive, 25% microinvasive), indicating that high ROS levels are an impediment to tumor progression.
evaluation: Claims C8, C124-C126, C179-C180 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3H and Table 1. The NAC treatment experiment provides important mechanistic insight by demonstrating that reducing ROS promotes tumor progression, supporting the therapeutic rationale of increasing ROS. This is consistent with recent literature (C179) showing dual roles of ROS in cancer.

result: HK2 expression is induced in PTEN-deficient prostate cancer cells in an Akt-dependent manner to increase glycolysis. PTEN-deficient PC3 and LNCaP cells expressed higher HK2 levels than PTEN-proficient DU145 cells. HK2 levels were dependent on Akt, as demonstrated by MK2206 treatment, Akt knockdown, and PTEN manipulation experiments.
evaluation: Claims C9-C10, C39, C135-C140, C181-C182 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5A and supplementary figures. The Akt-dependence of HK2 expression is demonstrated through multiple complementary approaches: pan-Akt inhibitor (C137), Akt1/2 knockdown (C138), PTEN knockdown (C139), and PTEN overexpression (C140). HK2 induction in mouse prostates after PTEN deletion (C182, Figure 6A) confirms in vivo relevance.

result: HK2 deficiency in PTEN-deficient prostate cancer markedly inhibited tumor development and extended lifespan through both cytostatic and cytotoxic mechanisms. In vitro, HK2 knockdown in PC3 and LNCaP cells (but not DU145) decreased hexokinase activity, impaired proliferation, and reduced anchorage-independent growth. In Pbsn-Cre4;Ptenf/f;Hk2f/f mice, HK2 deletion decreased prostate weights, inhibited proliferation, increased apoptosis, and substantially extended survival.
evaluation: Claims C11-C12, C43-C44, C141-C148, C159-C164 are supported by comprehensive in vitro (Figure 5B-F) and in vivo data (Figure 6). The cell line specificity (C146-C147) demonstrates selectivity for PTEN-deficient cells. The mouse model data (Figure 6B-E) showing both decreased proliferation and increased apoptosis supports both cytostatic and cytotoxic effects (C163-C164), which is notable compared to other cancer models (C187).

result: HK2 deficiency overcomes chemoresistance of PTEN-deficient prostate cancer cells to etoposide. PTEN-deficient cells are relatively resistant to etoposide due to Akt activation, but HK2 knockdown re-sensitized these cells. In xenograft studies, inducible HK2 knockdown substantially decreased tumor growth, and the combination of HK2 knockdown with etoposide prohibited tumor growth through decreased proliferation and increased cell death.
evaluation: Claims C45, C149-C153, C185-C186 are supported by in vitro data (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 6) and xenograft experiments (Figure 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 7). The data demonstrate that HK2 is required for Akt-mediated chemoresistance and that targeting HK2 can restore chemosensitivity. This provides a therapeutic strategy to overcome a major clinical challenge.

result: HK2 knockdown in PC3 cells significantly reduced glycolysis (ECAR) but was associated with a compensatory increase in oxygen consumption (OCR), leading to further increased ROS levels and enhanced sensitivity to PEITC-induced cell death. This suggests HK2 depletion combined with PEITC could be an additional therapeutic strategy.
evaluation: Claims C154-C158 are supported by metabolic flux data (Figure 5—figure supplement 8-9) and ROS/cell death measurements (Figure 5—figure supplement 10-11). The compensatory increase in OXPHO after glycolysis inhibition is an important mechanistic finding that explains the synergy with ROS inducers. This provides rationale for combining HK2 inhibition with PEITC.

result: Sestrin3 (Sesn3) expression pattern was consistent with ROS levels in prostate cancer cells, with DU145 cells expressing high Sesn3 and PC3/LNCaP cells expressing low Sesn3. Modulation of Sesn3 levels was sufficient to alter cytosolic ROS production, suggesting Sesn3 contributes to ROS regulation downstream of Akt and FoxOs.
evaluation: Claims C67-C72 are supported by expression data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and functional experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 4-5). Sesn3 knockdown in DU145 increased ROS (C70), while Sesn3 overexpression in PC3 decreased ROS (C71). However, the contribution of Sesn3 appears to be one of multiple mechanisms regulating ROS, as MnSOD and catalase did not correlate with ROS levels (C66).

result: Changes in MnSOD and catalase expression in prostate cancer cells did not correlate with changes in ROS levels, contrasting with previous findings in MEFs.
evaluation: Claim C66 is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and is consistent with previous observations (Chowdhury et al., 2007). This negative result is important as it indicates cell-type-specific mechanisms of ROS regulation and suggests Sesn3 may be more important than MnSOD/catalase in prostate cancer cells.

result: PEITC is a natural compound from cruciferous vegetables that increases intracellular ROS by depleting glutathione. 2-ME is an endogenous estradiol metabolite that increases ROS.
evaluation: Claims C38, C76-C78 represent established knowledge about these compounds supported by citations and confirmed by experimental data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) showing PEITC depletes glutathione. These are methodological details supporting the therapeutic approach.

result: LNCaP and PC3 cells are more vulnerable to the glutathione-reducing agent BSO, and the NADP+/NADPH ratio is elevated in PTEN-deficient cells.
evaluation: Claims C80-C81 are supported by experimental data (Figure 2—figure supplement 3-4). These findings provide additional mechanistic support for the vulnerability of PTEN-deficient cells to oxidative stress, though the authors note the elevated NADP+/NADPH ratio could be either cause or consequence of high ROS (C82-C84).

result: The elevated NADP+/NADPH ratio in PTEN-deficient cells could be contributing to high ROS, could result from increased NADPH consumption to combat high ROS, or could result from increased NADPH consumption for fatty acid synthesis.
evaluation: Claims C82-C84 are explicitly speculative ("could be") and represent alternative mechanistic hypotheses that are not distinguished by the current data. Additional experiments would be needed to determine which mechanism(s) explain the elevated NADP+/NADPH ratio. The authors appropriately present these as possibilities rather than conclusions.

result: Oxygen consumption and ROS production were increased by silencing PTEN in DU145 cells and decreased in PC3 and LNCaP cells expressing PTEN.
evaluation: Claims C88-C89 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 8. These gain- and loss-of-function experiments provide important validation that PTEN status causally determines oxygen consumption and ROS levels, supporting the mechanistic model.

result: The synergistic effect of rapamycin and PEITC on cell death could be explained by ROS induction exceeding scavenging capacity. Rapamycin itself does not substantially affect oxygen consumption or ROS, contrasting with the catalytic mTOR inhibitor torin1, consistent with differential effects on OXPHO via eIF4E.
evaluation: Claims C101-C104 are supported by experimental data (Figure 2—figure supplement 13-14) and citation to Morita et al., 2013. The mechanistic distinction between rapamycin (mTORC1-specific) and torin1 (catalytic inhibitor) is important for understanding why rapamycin synergizes with PEITC through Akt activation rather than by directly reducing OXPHO/ROS.

result: In PTEN-proficient DU145 xenografts, the effects of rapamycin alone or PEITC alone were not as profound as in PC3 xenografts, and the combination did not decrease tumor growth as effectively.
evaluation: Claims C111-C112 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 15. This negative control is important for demonstrating the selectivity of the therapeutic approach for PTEN-deficient tumors, though the sample size appears smaller than the PC3 xenograft study.

result: Knockdown of hexokinase 1 (HK1) in PC3 cells had only modest effects on total hexokinase activity and no effect on cell proliferation compared to HK2 knockdown.
evaluation: Claims C144-C145 are supported by experimental data (Figure 5—figure supplement 4-5). This control experiment is important for demonstrating the specificity of HK2's role in PTEN-deficient prostate cancer cells and ruling out general hexokinase dependence.

result: Background knowledge claims about Akt, PTEN, PI3K signaling, HK2, and the rationale for developing alternative therapeutic approaches to pan-Akt inhibition.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C13-C34, C40-C42, C54-C57, C63-C65, C165-C168, C178, C183, C188-C190, C192 represent established knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These provide necessary context and rationale for the study but are not novel findings. The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are consistent with the field.

result: Summary and concluding statements about the therapeutic approaches developed in this study.
evaluation: Claims C184, C191, C193 are summary statements and conclusions that are supported by the collective experimental evidence presented in the manuscript. C184 is an inference about Akt increasing HK2 activity through phosphorylation-mediated mitochondrial binding, which is reasonable based on cited work and the data shown. C191 and C193 appropriately summarize the two therapeutic strategies validated in the study.
